name: Bioregionalism
summary: Bioregionalism holds that human life should be organised around natural regions defined by watersheds, soils, flora and fauna, not by arbitrary political borders. It favours decentralized self-governing communities federated with one another, regional economic self-reliance, a steady-state economy and appropriate technology, and it treats industrial capitalism and the nation-state as the root of ecological and social crisis. It draws on indigenous place-based traditions and on ecofeminism and earth spirituality.
scope: The North American bioregional movement from Peter Berg, Gary Snyder and Jim Dodge to Kirkpatrick Sale's Dwellers in the Land and the continental congresses (as Doug Aberley's survey and Sale's 1983 lecture set them out), with the scholarly essays in McGinnis (ed.) 1999 for context. It excludes bioregional planning as a technical discipline and the scholars' own proposals in that volume. No state applied it, so there is no record beyond the movement's words and its congress procedures.

decide-locally.rationale: Sale makes decentralization, division and diversity the political principles of a bioregion, in contrast to giantism and centralization, and Aberley's tenets name decentralized governance with subsidiarity as the basis of sustainability.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Aberley's tenets call bioregional governance democratic and participatory, and Sale lists town-meeting democracy and local control among the traditional values bioregionalism revives, though he adds that autonomous regions may choose other systems.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Aberley's synthesis of the movement's tenets says humans and other species have an intrinsic right to coevolve, and Sale rejects any species ruling over the others.

limit-growth.rationale: Sale says a bioregional economy aims at a steady state and conservation instead of perpetual change and continual growth, which he calls a false goddess.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Sale quotes Schumacher that no technological progress could solve the life-and-death problems of industrial society, and rejects technofix visions of the future.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Aberley's tenets name industrial capitalism and machine-based civilization as the root cause of the ecological and social crises, and Sale treats the industrial system as bound to collapse and its practices as demonic.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Aberley's tenets expect networks of federation between autonomous bioregions, and Dodge's anarchic structure rests on federated self-reliant communities, which fits coordination without a ruling centre.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Bioregional governance is described as autonomous and drawn from the region's own nature, which cannot be squared with self-government resting on powers a national legislature may withdraw.

state-harmful.rationale: Dodge describes an anarchic structure of governance and Sale links the movement to anarchism, yet Aberley's tenets and Sale's own scheme set up bioregional governments, so the strands split on the state itself.

right-to-secede.rationale: Berg argues that the northern California bioregion should be a separate state, not administered by a larger one, and Sale presents separatist movements as an early form of bioregional society.

political-borders-follow-ecosystems.rationale: Sale defines a bioregion by natural rather than human boundaries, and Snyder in the founding texts quoted by Aberley calls for division by natural and cultural boundaries rather than arbitrary political ones.

local-production.rationale: Sale makes self-sufficiency the elemental principle of a bioregional economy, finding energy, food, shelter, clothing and manufacture within the bioregion, and Aberley's tenets favour locally manufactured goods and cooperative self-reliance.

free-trade.rationale: Sale holds that a bioregion avoids elaborate networks of continental dependency and Aberley counts globalization as a politics of displacement, so free trade is not held to benefit all.

simple-living.rationale: Sale says a bioregional economy would minimize resource use and be self-sufficient, and Snyder's founding statement names overconsumption among the root conditions of the crisis.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Snyder's founding essay, as Aberley quotes it, counts overconsumption among the root conditions of the crisis and Aberley sets bioregional culture against the consumer-producer society.

limit-population.rationale: Snyder's founding statement, quoted by Aberley, names overpopulation as a root condition and envisions a human population much smaller than today's.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Sale's bioregional society keeps cities of up to 100,000 and agriculture, and Aberley describes newly indigenous cultures using appropriate technology, not a return to hunting and gathering.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Sale says the bioregional vision has nothing to do with nuclear fission, which he calls the most unnatural project humankind has devised.

space-expansion.rationale: Sale lists rockets full of people and space colonies among the violent technofix visions that bioregionalism does not share.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Sale asks for slow, steady change and rejects technofix visions, and Aberley favours appropriate technology tied to ecological design, not faster disruptive change.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Sale's vision rests on a principle of nonexploitation and reverence for all creatures, and Aberley gives other species a right to coevolve.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Aberley's tenets support ceremony and spiritual reflection as part of bioregional culture, and Sale casts the goal as a change of consciousness toward the earth as sacred.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Aberley reports that bioregionalism embraces ecofeminism and quotes approvingly Fike and Kerr on the links between feminism, environmentalism and other freedom struggles.

democracy-best.rationale: Aberley's tenets call bioregional governance democratic, while Sale expects and accepts that autonomous bioregions will run aristocracies, theocracies and other systems.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: The North American Bioregional Congress, the movement's own assembly, adopted its policies in twenty-three areas by consensus, as Aberley records.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Sale follows Schumacher that the market economy errs against nature and wants a bioregion to plan and allocate its own resources.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Sale names gradualism a virtue of bioregionalism, with change steady and slow, not by revolutionary decree or legislative fiat.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Sale says bioregionalism joins, or ignores, right and left, uniting communards with hunters and blunting lesser political differences.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Sale quotes Schumacher that the guidance needed cannot be found in science or technology but in traditional wisdom, and holds that wisdom arises in the soul as an emanation of the earth spirit.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Berg names the supremacy of some cultures over others, and of some human beings over others, as an assumption that produces globalist monoculture, and sets against it a common human identity and regional diversity.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Berg holds that all human beings share a common identity as one species and rejects the supremacy of some human beings over others.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Berg condemns Europe's rule over the Americas, Africa and Asia as terrestrial piracy and the imposition of an alien world-view, and sets regional self-determination against it.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Berg describes colonial rule that skims the cream off captive territories as domination and piracy, which he rejects.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Berg describes the colonists of North America as invaders who displaced and annihilated the native peoples, and the United States as a nation born of that takeover.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: Berg condemns the removal and extermination of native peoples from their lands as a tradition of scrubbing human inhabitants out of living places.

population-transfer.rationale: Berg names displacement of peoples from their regions as fatal and counts forced removals among the crimes of the colonial order.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: Berg names displacement of peoples from their regions as fatal and counts forced removals among the crimes of the colonial order.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Berg treats the United States' growth from coast to coast and its wars of conquest as a steamroll of destruction, the opposite of living in place.

national-mission.rationale: Berg calls the Myth of the West a biocidal beacon and attacks the patriotic fervor of the 1976 bicentennial and the spreading of one world-view over other regions.

patriotic-education.rationale: Berg wrote his manifesto to counter the patriotic fervor of the 1976 Bicentennial and calls the American nation's founding a declaration with no regard for the land.

civilizational-union.rationale: Berg rejects the United West as a state of mind built on displacement and Sale welcomes the world breaking into smaller units, so uniting nations by civilization runs against their scheme.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Sale welcomes the refragmenting of states into smaller regional units and treats decentralization as the trend of the age, which runs against uniting peoples across borders into larger blocs.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Sale holds that the reach and power of governments must shrink and he blames transnational governments for placing regions at the mercy of distant bureaucracies.

revolution-justified.rationale: Sale says a bioregional civilization will not come by revolutionary decree, no matter whose, but by slow, steady evolution, while Berg's own project is reinhabitation, not seizure of power.

gradual-change.rationale: Sale names gradualism a virtue of bioregionalism and Aberley describes resistance and renewal carried on within and alongside existing power structures.
